summary: Describes a hierarchical architecture of stateful PCEs, where a parent PCE coordinates child PCEs that each manage a part of the network. It sets out the requirements and procedures for computing traffic-engineered paths across multiple domains while keeping state.

eli5.summary: A big school has one head teacher who coordinates classroom teachers. Here a main route planner coordinates smaller planners for different parts of a network.

questions: how do stateful pces work across domains
how does hierarchical stateful pce work
how do parent and child pces communicate
when is stateful hierarchical pce used
subtitle: Parent and child route planners working together to find paths across multiple network domains.

tldr.problem: Networks often span multiple domains controlled by different operators, and each domain has its own path planning system. A single route planner cannot see inside other domains to find the best cross-domain paths.
tldr.mechanism: A parent route planner coordinates with child route planners in each domain, maintaining state about current paths and resources. It can compute end-to-end paths, delegate control of paths to child planners, and initiate new paths across domains.
tldr.outcome: Stateful hierarchy allows better coordination in multi-domain networks like those used in data centers and wide-area traffic engineering. The RFC builds on prior work in hierarchical PCEs and stateful PCEs.

facts.label: Coordination model
facts.value: Parent PCE coordinates multiple child PCEs

facts.label: Hierarchy depth
facts.value: Recursive: child can delegate to parent, parent to grandparent

facts.label: Security recommendations
facts.value: TLS or TCP-AO for PCEP sessions

today: RFC 8751 is an Informational document that describes best practices for stateful hierarchical PCEs. It builds on RFC 6805 (hierarchical PCE) and RFC 8231 (stateful PCE), both of which are normative references. The techniques are used in ACTN deployments and multi-domain traffic engineering.

sections.title: How Hierarchical Stateful PCE Works
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) is a system that plans traffic-engineered paths through a network. A stateful PCE remembers the current state of the network: which paths are active, what resources they are using, and what path requests are pending. This state allows it to compute new paths while avoiding collisions with existing ones.

When a network spans multiple domains (separate administrative or technical regions), a hierarchical PCE architecture helps: a parent PCE (P-PCE) maintains a map of how the domains connect and coordinates with child PCEs (C-PCEs) that each manage one or more domains. Combining stateful capability with hierarchy means the parent PCE can track interdomain paths and resources globally, while each child PCE optimizes paths within its domain.
sections.eli5: The head teacher (parent PCE) keeps a notebook of all lessons across all classrooms (interdomain paths). The classroom teachers (child PCEs) report what they are teaching and ask the head teacher for help scheduling lessons that move between classrooms.

sections.title: Three Modes of Operation
sections.content:
Stateful hierarchical PCEs operate in three modes:

Passive mode uses the procedures of RFC 6805: when a PCC (Path Computation Client, such as a router) requests an end-to-end path, the ingress child PCE forwards the request to the parent PCE. The parent selects candidate domain paths, asks each child PCE for path segments across its domain, and concatenates them. The child PCE also reports the status of the resulting LSP back to the parent, so the parent knows the current state of interdomain paths.

Active mode extends passive mode: the child PCE grants the parent PCE the right to modify an LSP (delegation). The parent PCE can send update requests to the child PCE, which propagates them to the PCC. This allows the parent to reroute paths in response to topology changes or LSP state changes.

PCE-initiated mode allows the parent PCE to request that a child PCE initiate a new LSP. The child PCE receives the request and instructs the ingress router (PCC) to set up the path. Paths can be set up as single end-to-end LSPs or as stitched per-domain segments.
sections.eli5: In passive mode, a teacher reports: 'I started the lesson from room A to C.' In active mode, the head teacher can say, 'Change the lesson path from room A to D instead.' In initiated mode, the head teacher says, 'Start a new lesson from room A to room E,' and the teacher makes it happen.

sections.title: Messages Between PCEs
sections.content:
Stateful hierarchical PCEs exchange messages using PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol). The extensions from RFC 8231 (stateful PCE) and RFC 8685 (hierarchical PCE) define the messages used. A PCEP speaker must advertise both stateful and hierarchical capabilities in its Open message.

Key message types include: LSP State Report (PCRpt) sent by a child PCE to report the state of LSPs; LSP Control Delegation (with the D flag) sent by a child PCE to grant the parent PCE control over an LSP; LSP Update Request (PCUpd) sent by the parent PCE to modify an LSP; and LSP Initiate Request (PCInitiate) sent by the parent PCE to request a new LSP. These messages form a recursive hierarchy: a child PCE can delegate to its parent, which can delegate to its own parent.
sections.eli5: Teachers send notes to the head teacher saying 'LSP 5 is now UP' or 'Please take over LSP 5' or 'I started LSP 10 as you asked.' The notes follow a standard form so they are always understood correctly.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes two major deployment contexts: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks), where the parent PCE acts as a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC) and child PCEs act as Provisioning Network Controllers (PNCs); and interlayer traffic engineering, where separate PCEs coordinate paths in different network layers (e.g., optical and IP).

Key considerations include security and confidentiality: child domains must not expose their internal topology to the parent. Path-keys (from RFC 5520) can hide path segment details. PCEP sessions between parent and child PCEs SHOULD use TLS or TCP-AO for security. Scalability requires that child PCEs only report LSPs that are either delegated to or initiated by the parent, not every LSP in the domain. State synchronization mechanisms from RFC 8232 apply to parent-child sessions as well as client-PCE sessions.
sections.eli5: When teachers and the head teacher first connect, they make sure they can trust each other's messages. Teachers do not announce every lesson plan, only the ones the head teacher asked for. The head teacher keeps a record that can be recovered if messages are lost.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The security considerations from RFC 8231, RFC 6805, and RFC 5440 apply. The parent PCE SHOULD require all child PCEs to use the strongest available PCEP security (TLS or TCP-AO). Any multidomain operation risks exposing information across domain boundaries, especially when domains are controlled by different organizations. The hierarchical architecture is designed to minimize this risk by keeping internal domain topology hidden from the parent.

Path-keys allow a child PCE to replace a path segment with an opaque key, hiding its contents from the parent. LSP state reports must maintain internal domain confidentiality. A child PCE can withdraw delegation if it detects a topology change inside its domain that the parent does not know about, or the parent can request delegation if it needs to make a change to an LSP.
sections.eli5: The head teacher must trust the teachers. Teachers can hide details about their lessons (paths) if those lessons are confidential. If something changes inside a classroom that the head teacher does not know about, the teacher takes back control until the head teacher is informed.
